title: "Water safety profiles and infant mortality in Colombian municipalities, 2016-2023"
author: "Water-quality workshop"
abstract: |
  We describe how Colombian municipalities group by drinking-water safety and context,
  using real public data. K-means on nine standardised profile features, including the
  utility-supplied IRCA, finds four clusters. Infant mortality, Saber 11 scores and school
  dropout are used only to describe the clusters, never to form them. Within clusters the
  association between IRCA and infant mortality is weak. All comparisons are descriptive
  and do not establish a causal effect of water safety.

```{python}
import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
prof = pd.read_csv("outputs/cluster_profiles.csv").set_index("cluster")
oy = pd.read_csv("outputs/outcomes_by_year.csv")
bins = pd.read_csv("outputs/irca_infant_bins.csv")
rho = pd.read_csv("outputs/irca_infant.csv").set_index("cluster")
ks = pd.read_csv("outputs/k_selection.csv")
S = json.load(open("outputs/summary.json"))
names = prof["name"]
```

# Introduction

Safe drinking water is a precondition for child health, yet water safety varies widely
across Colombian municipalities and between urban and rural zones. The national
surveillance index IRCA (*Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua*) runs from 0 (no risk) to
100 (unfit) and is classified into bands by Resolución 2115 de 2007 [@res2115]. The open
INS table used here reports the **utility-supplied ("prestadores") IRCA** [@ins_irca], not
INS's national total. We ask how municipalities group by water safety and context, and how
outcomes look in each group.

# Methods

The unit of analysis is a municipality x zone (urban or rural) x year row, 2016-2023, built
from public sources [@ins_irca; @terridata; @dane; @icfes; @men; @funk2026; @chirps3data; @srtm2013].
We keep rows of municipalities with an IRCA value (`{python} f"{S['kept']:,}"` rows,
`{python} f"{S['municipalities']:,}"` municipalities). For department capitals, which have no
urban/rural coverage split, urban coverage is filled from the municipal total
(`{python} S['capital_urban_rows_filled_from_total']` flagged rows).

Each of nine profile features $x_{ij}$ is standardised within year,
$$
z_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \bar{x}_{j,t(i)}}{s_{j,t(i)}},
$$ {#eq-z}

where $\bar{x}_{j,t(i)}$ and $s_{j,t(i)}$ are the mean and standard deviation of feature $j$
in the year $t(i)$ of row $i$. K-means [@lloyd1982] minimises the within-cluster sum of squares

$$
W = \sum_{c=1}^{k} \sum_{i \in C_c} \lVert z_i - m_c \rVert^2 ,
$$ {#eq-kmeans}

with $m_c$ the centroid of cluster $C_c$. We choose $k$ by the elbow of @eq-kmeans and the
silhouette [@rousseeuw1987]

$$
s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max\{a(i), b(i)\}},
$$ {#eq-silhouette}

where $a(i)$ is the mean distance to the other points of its cluster and $b(i)$ the smallest
mean distance to another cluster. Stability across seeds is measured with the adjusted Rand
index [@hubert1985]. Outcomes are never used for clustering.

```{python}
#| label: fig-selection
#| fig-cap: "Inertia (left) and mean silhouette (right) by number of clusters k."
#| fig-alt: "Two line charts against k from 2 to 8: inertia falling and flattening after four clusters, and the silhouette score peaking at k = 2 with similar low values for larger k."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 2.6))
ax[0].plot(ks["k"], ks["inertia"], marker="o"); ax[0].set_xlabel("k"); ax[0].set_ylabel("inertia")
ax[1].plot(ks["k"], ks["silhouette"], marker="o", color="tab:orange"); ax[1].set_xlabel("k"); ax[1].set_ylabel("silhouette")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

# Results

We selected $k$ = `{python} S['k']`: the next cluster lowers inertia by only about 7%, the
silhouette is `{python} round(S['silhouette_at_k'], 2)` and the adjusted Rand index across five seeds
is at least `{python} round(S['ari_min'], 3)`. The clusters are
"`{python} '", "'.join(names)`". @fig-heatmap shows what separates them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Cluster mean z-scores (within year) of the nine profile features."
#| fig-alt: "Heatmap with nine profile features as rows and four named clusters as columns, coloured from blue (below average) to red (above)."
zc = [c for c in prof.columns if c.startswith("z_")]
M = prof[zc].T; M.index = [c[2:] for c in zc]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
v = np.abs(M.values).max()
im = ax.imshow(M.values, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-v, vmax=v, aspect="auto")
ax.set_xticks(range(M.shape[1])); ax.set_xticklabels([names[c].replace(", ", ",\n") for c in M.columns], fontsize=6)
ax.set_yticks(range(M.shape[0])); ax.set_yticklabels(M.index, fontsize=7)
for i in range(M.shape[0]):
    for j in range(M.shape[1]):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{M.values[i, j]:.1f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6)
fig.colorbar(im, label="mean z-score"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

@fig-outcomes shows the outcomes by cluster; lines break in years without data.

```{python}
#| label: fig-outcomes
#| fig-cap: "Median infant mortality per 1,000 live births, Saber 11 score and school dropout (%) by cluster and year."
#| fig-alt: "Three line charts of outcomes by year for four clusters, with gaps where a source has no data."
years = np.arange(2016, 2024)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.5, 2.8))
for ax, o in zip(axes, ["infant_mortality", "saber11_mean", "dropout_rate"]):
    for c, g in oy[oy["outcome"] == o].groupby("cluster"):
        ax.plot(years, g.set_index("year")["median"].reindex(years).values, marker="o", ms=2,
                color=prof.loc[c, "color"], label=names[c])
    ax.set_title(o, fontsize=8); ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)
fig.legend(*axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="lower center", ncol=2, fontsize=5)
plt.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.15, 1, 1)); plt.show()
```

Within clusters, Spearman's $\rho$ between IRCA and infant mortality ranges from
`{python} f"{rho['spearman_rho'].min():.2f}"` to `{python} f"{rho['spearman_rho'].max():.2f}"`,
a weak association.

# Conclusions

Municipal water-safety profiles form four descriptive groups. Their outcome differences
mirror poverty, rurality and altitude as much as IRCA, and within clusters the IRCA-infant
mortality association is weak. This is not evidence that water quality does or does not
cause any outcome. Limits: utility-supplied IRCA only, rural zones often unsampled, imputed
coverage, a change of infant-mortality method in 2017 and no Saber 11 data for 2018 and 2021.
